title: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm, Partners for Life
text:
Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm were born a year apart, in 1785 and 1786, in Hanau. When their father died in 1796, the family fell into poverty, and as the eldest sons they took responsibility for their mother and younger siblings. They studied law at Marburg and became fascinated by old German literature.

From 1806 they began collecting folk tales, from books and from storytellers such as Dorothea Viehmann, a tailor's wife who sold produce at market and knew dozens of stories. In December 1812 they published the first volume of Children's and Household Tales. Wilhelm, the gentler stylist, kept revising the tales through seven editions until 1857, while Jacob devoted himself more to the history of language, describing the regular sound shifts of the Germanic languages that are still called Grimm's law.

The brothers lived and worked together nearly all their lives. When Wilhelm married Dorothea Wild in 1825, Jacob, who never married, simply lived on in their household. In 1837 both lost their professorships at Gottingen because they joined five colleagues in protesting against the King of Hanover's abolition of the constitution. In 1841 they moved to Berlin, where they carried on the vast German Dictionary they had begun together in 1838.

Wilhelm died in 1859 and Jacob in 1863, still working on the letter F. Scholars finished the dictionary in 1961.
lesson: Siblings who keep working side by side can build something neither could finish alone. A shared life's project is a powerful bond.
people: Jacob Grimm, Wilhelm Grimm, Dorothea Viehmann
source: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmarchen (1812 to 1857); Jack Zipes, The Brothers Grimm (1988)
